{{short description|Well-spaced set of points in a metric space}}
[[File:Metric epsilon-net.svg|thumb|300px|The red points form part of an {{mvar|ε}}-net for the [[Euclidean plane]], where {{mvar|ε}} is the radius of the large yellow disks. The blue disks of half the radius are [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]], and the yellow disks together cover the whole plane, satisfying the two definitional requirements on an {{mvar|ε}}-net.]]

In the mathematical theory of [[metric space]]s, ''' {{mvar|ε}}-nets''', ''' {{mvar|ε}}-packings''', ''' {{mvar|ε}}-coverings''', '''uniformly discrete sets''', '''relatively dense sets''', and '''Delone sets''' (named after [[Boris Delone]]) are several closely related definitions of well-spaced [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] of points, and the '''packing radius''' and '''covering radius''' of these sets measure how well-spaced they are. These sets have applications in [[coding theory]], [[approximation algorithm]]s, and the theory of [[quasicrystal]]s.

== Definitions ==
If {{math|(''M'', ''d'')}} is a metric space, and {{mvar|X}} is a subset of {{mvar|M}}, then the '''packing radius''', {{mvar|r}}, of {{mvar|X}} is half of the [[infimum]] of distances between distinct members of {{mvar|X}}. [[Ball (mathematics)|Open balls]] of radius {{mvar|r}} centered at the points of {{mvar|X}} will all be disjoint from each other. The '''covering radius''', {{mvar|R}}, of {{mvar|X}} is the smallest distance such that every point of {{mvar|M}} is within distance {{mvar|R}} of at least one point in {{mvar|X}}; that is, {{mvar|R}} is the smallest radius such that [[Ball (mathematics)|closed balls]] of that radius centered at the points of {{mvar|X}} have all of {{mvar|M}} as their union. 

An ''' {{mvar|ε}}-packing''' is a set {{mvar|X}} of packing radius {{math|''r'' ≥ ''ε''/2}} (equivalently, minimum distance {{math|≥ ''ε''}}), an '''{{mvar|ε}}-covering''' is a set {{mvar|X}} of covering radius {{math|''R'' ≤ ''ε''}}, and an ''' {{mvar|ε}}-net''' is a set that is both an {{mvar|ε}}-packing and an {{mvar|ε}}-covering ({{math|''ε''/2 ≤ ''r'' ≤ ''R'' ≤ ''ε''}}). 

A set is '''uniformly discrete''' if it has a nonzero packing radius ({{math|0 < ''r''}}), and '''relatively dense''' if it has a finite covering radius ({{math|''R'' < ∞}}). 

A '''Delone set''' is a set that is both uniformly discrete and relatively dense ({{math|0 < ''r'' ≤ ''R'' < ∞}}). Thus every {{mvar|ε}}-net is Delone, but not vice versa.<ref>

== Construction of ''ε''-nets ==
As the most restrictive of the definitions above, {{mvar|ε}}-nets are at least as difficult to construct as {{mvar|ε}}-packings, {{mvar|ε}}-coverings, and Delone sets. However, whenever the points of {{mvar|M}} have a [[well-ordering]], [[transfinite induction]] shows that it is possible to construct an {{mvar|ε}}-net {{mvar|N}}, by including in {{mvar|N}} every point for which the infimum of distances to the set of earlier points in the ordering is at least&nbsp;{{mvar|ε}}. For finite sets of points in a Euclidean space of bounded dimension, each point may be tested in constant time by mapping it to a grid of cells of diameter {{mvar|ε}}, and using a [[hash table]] to test which nearby cells already contain points of {{mvar|N}}; thus, in this case, an {{mvar|ε}}-net can be constructed in [[linear time]].<ref>

 | journal = [[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]

 | title = Clustering motion
 | volume = 31

}}</ref><ref>

For more general finite or [[compact space|compact]] metric spaces, an alternative algorithm of [[Teofilo F. Gonzalez|Teo Gonzalez]] based on the [[farthest-first traversal]] can be used to construct a finite {{mvar|ε}}-net. This algorithm initializes the net {{mvar|N}} to be empty, and then repeatedly adds to {{mvar|N}} the farthest point in {{mvar|M}} from {{mvar|N}}, breaking ties arbitrarily and stopping when all points of&nbsp;{{mvar|M}} are within distance&nbsp;{{mvar|ε}} of&nbsp;{{mvar|N}}.<ref>

}}</ref> In [[doubling space|spaces of bounded doubling dimension]], Gonzalez' algorithm can be implemented in {{math|O(''n'' log ''n'')}} time for point sets with a polynomial ratio between their farthest and closest distances, and approximated in the same time bound for arbitrary point sets.<ref name="HM06">

== Applications ==
=== Coding theory ===
{{main|Hamming bound#Covering radius and packing radius}}

In the theory of [[error-correcting code]]s, the metric space containing a [[block code]] {{mvar|C}} consists of strings of a fixed length, say {{mvar|n}}, taken over an alphabet of size {{mvar|q}} (can be thought of as [[Coordinate vector|vectors]]), with the [[Hamming metric]]. This space is denoted by {{tmath|\mathcal{A}_q^n.}} The covering radius and packing radius of this metric space are related to the code's ability to correct errors. An example is provided by the [[Berlekamp switching game]].

=== Approximation algorithms ===
{{harvtxt|Har-Peled|Raichel|2013}} describe an algorithmic paradigm that they call "net and prune" for designing [[approximation algorithm]]s for certain types of geometric optimization problems defined on sets of points in [[Euclidean space]]s. An algorithm of this type works by performing the following steps:
# Choose a random point {{mvar|p}} from the point set, find its nearest neighbor {{mvar|q}}, and set {{mvar|ε}} to the distance between {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}}.
# Test whether {{mvar|ε}} is (approximately) bigger than or smaller than the optimal solution value (using a technique specific to the particular optimization problem being solved)
#* If it is bigger, remove from the input the points whose closest neighbor is farther than {{mvar|ε}}
#* If it is smaller, construct an {{mvar|ε}}-net {{mvar|N}}, and remove from the input the points that are not in {{mvar|N}}.
In both cases, the expected number of remaining points decreases by a constant factor, so the time is dominated by the testing step. As they show, this paradigm can be used to construct fast approximation algorithms for [[k-center]] clustering, finding a pair of points with median distance, and several related problems.

A hierarchical system of nets, called a ''net-tree'', may be used in [[doubling space|spaces of bounded doubling dimension]] to construct [[well-separated pair decomposition]]s, [[geometric spanner]]s, and approximate [[Nearest neighbor search|nearest neighbors]].<ref name="HM06"/><ref>

=== Crystallography ===
For points in [[Euclidean space]], a set {{mvar|X}} is a [[Meyer set]] if it is relatively dense and its [[Minkowski difference|difference set]] {{math|''X'' &minus; ''X''}} is uniformly discrete. Equivalently, {{mvar|X}} is a Meyer set if both {{mvar|X}} and {{math|''X'' &minus; ''X''}} are Delone sets. Meyer sets are named after [[Yves Meyer]], who introduced them (with a different but equivalent definition based on [[harmonic analysis]]) as a mathematical model for [[quasicrystal]]s. They include the point sets of [[lattice (group)|lattice]]s, [[Penrose tiling]]s, and the [[Minkowski sum]]s of these sets with finite sets.<ref>
